How bail bond
companies make money

lines.text: The bondsman keeps your $2,000 even when you show up.
lines.say: The bondsman keeps your two thousand dollars even when you show up.

lines.text: Say bail is $20,000. A bondsman often charges 10%, or $2,000, and you don't get it back.
lines.say: Say bail is twenty thousand dollars. A bondsman often charges ten percent, or two thousand, and you don't get it back.

lines.text: The insurer backing the bond typically takes about 10% of that fee. The agent keeps most of the rest, but covers losses.
lines.say: The insurer backing the bond typically takes about ten percent of that fee. The agent keeps most of the rest, but covers losses.

lines.text: The catch for the agent: if you skip court, they can owe the full $20,000.
lines.say: The catch for the agent: if you skip court, they can owe the full twenty thousand.

lines.text: So agents ask for collateral and co-signers, and track down people who miss court.
lines.say: So agents ask for collateral and co-signers, and track down people who miss court.

lines.text: In big US counties, surety bonds rose from 24% of felony releases in 1990-94 to 42% in 2002-04.
lines.say: In big US counties, surety bonds rose from twenty-four to forty-two percent of felony releases by the mid two-thousands.

post.title: How bail bond companies make money: the 10% fee
post.ig:
The bondsman keeps your $2,000 even when you show up.
On $20,000 bail, agents often charge a nonrefundable 10% fee: $2,000.
The insurer backing the bond typically takes about 10% of the fee; the agent keeps most of the rest, but can owe the full $20,000 if you skip court.
In the 75 largest US counties, surety bonds went from 24% of felony releases (1990-94) to 42% (2002-04).
Sources: Bureau of Justice Statistics (2007 report); California Department of Insurance; PolitiFact (2018). Rules vary by state.
